TASK ID: three-sat-to-clique

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Clique. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-SAT and TARGET is Clique. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = Clique
Clique.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a clique of AT LEAST k vertices: k vertices with an
edge between every two of them.

Edge cases: k <= 0 is always yes. k = 1 is yes whenever n >= 1. k > n is
always no.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-gvtljo5p
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

You may read files such as problems.py, but do not run, execute or test any code. Write reduce.py, then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.
Every reply must contain exactly one bash tool call. When you are done, finish by running exactly: echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT

function.arguments:
{"command":"cd /tmp/reduction-gvtljo5p && cat <<'EOF' > reduce.py
"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT (ThreeSat) to Clique.

Gadget construction (standard):
  * For every clause and every one of its three literals, create one vertex.
    Vertices are numbered 0..3*C-1, where C is the number of clauses.
  * Two vertices are joined by an edge iff they come from different clauses
    and their literals are not complementary (i.e. not v and -v).
  * Set k = C, the number of clauses.

Correctness:
  (=>) A satisfying assignment makes at least one literal true in each
       clause. Pick one true literal per clause; these C vertices lie in
       pairwise different clauses and no two are complementary (a variable
       cannot be both true and false), so they form a clique of size C.
  (<=) A clique of size C must contain at most one vertex per clause (no
       edges inside a clause) and there are exactly C clauses, hence exactly
       one vertex per clause. Since no two chosen literals are complementary,
       the assignment that sets each chosen literal true (and all other
       variables arbitrarily, e.g. false) is consistent and satisfies every
       clause. Thus a clique of size >= C exists iff the formula is
       satisfiable.

Edge case: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable. The reduction then
returns n = 0, edges = [], k = 0, and k <= 0 is always a yes-instance of
Clique, matching the source answer.

The construction uses O(C) vertices and O(C^2) edges, so it runs in
polynomial time and never calls a solver.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    """Reduce a ThreeSat instance to a Clique instance."""
    clauses = instance["clauses"]
    num_clauses = len(clauses)

    # No clauses: satisfiable. Return the empty graph with k = 0 (always yes).
    if num_clauses == 0:
        return {"n": 0, "edges": [], "k": 0}

    # One vertex per literal occurrence. vertex_literal[i] is the signed
    # literal represented by vertex i; vertex_clause[i] is its clause index.
    vertex_literal = []
    vertex_clause = []
    for ci, clause in enumerate(clauses):
        for lit in clause:
            vertex_literal.append(int(lit))
            vertex_clause.append(ci)

    n = len(vertex_literal)

    edges = []
    for i in range(n):
        li = vertex_literal[i]
        ci = vertex_clause[i]
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            # No edge within the same clause: a clique takes at most one
            # literal per clause.
            if ci == vertex_clause[j]:
                continue
            # No edge between complementary literals.
            if li == -vertex_literal[j]:
                continue
            edges.append([i, j])

    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": num_clauses}
EOF
